analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury, with most allowances going to households.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill; it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee from January 25, 2005 until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor action despite 18 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to set hard national caps on four pollutants from power plants: sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury, with the carbon and acid-rain caps to take effect in 2010 and the mercury cap in 2009. Power plants could trade emission allowances to meet the caps, but most of the allowances were set aside for households rather than given to industry, with declining shares reserved for transition aid to laid-off utility and coal workers and to electricity-intensive manufacturers. The committee it was assigned to never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to power plant pollution, especially downwind communities, asthma and heart-disease patients, and people who eat fish contaminated with mercury. Household electricity customers would also have received a share of the emission allowances to offset higher electricity prices, and workers and communities hurt by coal plant retirements would have gotten transition assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind communities, fish consumers, households, laid-off coal workers

how_it_helps.text: Sets national annual caps for 2010 and later of 2.25 million tons of sulfur dioxide, 1.51 million tons of nitrogen oxides, 2.05 billion tons of carbon dioxide, and a 5-ton mercury cap starting in 2009, with the sulfur dioxide caps split into separate western and nonwestern regional limits so upwind plants cannot trade their way out of downwind pollution.

After reserving shares for transition aid and clean energy, allocates all remaining emission allowances to electricity customers by household size, with trustees appointed to sell the allowances at fair market value and distribute the proceeds, so the value of the right to pollute goes to the public rather than to industry.

Reserves 6 percent of allowances in 2010, declining to 1.5 percent by 2019, for transition assistance to dislocated workers and hard-hit communities, including training, income-maintenance payments, and local economic development grants.
Reserves up to 20 percent of allowances for renewable generators, energy-efficient buildings, products, and projects, and cleaner fossil units, creating a revenue stream for low-carbon energy.

Treats mercury differently from tradeable pollutants: a strict rate limit of 2.48 grams per 1,000 megawatt-hours, an annual national review with mandatory tightening if the cap is exceeded, and rules requiring captured mercury to be permanently kept out of the air, groundwater, and agricultural land.
Contains a backstop: if the EPA failed to issue implementing regulations, every covered plant would have to meet steep percentage-based cuts on its own by 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning electric utilities, which would face compliance costs and would have to buy allowances beyond the shrinking free transition share, and their customers in coal-heavy states through higher electricity prices. Coal mining companies would face weaker demand for their product.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-burning utilities, their ratepayers, and coal miners

drawbacks.text: The emission caps would raise the cost of generating electricity from coal, and those costs would flow to customers as higher electricity prices, with the sharpest effects in coal-dependent regions, even though the household allowance allocation would partially offset them.

Power plants would receive free transition allocations for a decade based on their 2003 output, which compensates the largest historical emitters; supporters of auctioning all allowances would call this an unnecessary concession.

An allowance trading system concentrates emissions wherever allowances are cheapest, which the bill itself acknowledges by requiring studies of local air quality around trading plants and authorizing extra local limits if trading causes adverse local impacts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's public health case was strong: it targeted acid rain, mercury, and carbon dioxide from a single industry with hard caps, a strict mercury rule with no trading, and most of the allowance value routed to households rather than to plant owners. The real cost is higher electricity prices for coal-dependent regions, partially offset by the household dividend and worker transition aid. As designed, it gave away less to incumbents than most cap-and-trade proposals and came with an automatic backstop if regulators stalled. On balance the benefits outweighed the costs, though the burden would have fallen unevenly on coal communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator James Jeffords, an independent from Vermont, introduced the Clean Power Act of 2005 on January 25, 2005 with 18 cosponsors: 16 Democrats and 2 Republicans (Susan Collins and Olympia Snowe of Maine).

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced; the committee record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The committee was chaired at the time by Senator James Inhofe of Oklahoma, a coal-state ally and prominent skeptic of climate legislation, who took no action on the bill.

The Bush administration had put forward its own competing air-pollution plan, the Clear Skies initiative, which covered sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury but deliberately excluded carbon dioxide, giving the Republican-led committee an alternative to the Jeffords approach that avoided the central issue of climate emissions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities and the coal mining industry came out ahead: they avoided emission caps, allowance costs, and the strict mercury rule, while household customers never received the allowance dividend and downwind communities got no relief. The Bush administration's preferred no-carbon-cap approach remained in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities and the coal industry

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan on paper: 16 Democrats, 2 Maine Republicans, and 1 independent cosponsored the bill, but because no vote ever occurred the partisan split shows up instead in process, with a Republican committee chair taking no action and the Republican administration backing a narrower competing plan.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed hard caps on their sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon dioxide, and mercury emissions and required them to buy allowances beyond a small, declining free share. The industry's interest in avoiding these costs runs directly against the public health benefits the caps would deliver.

Carbon caps and strict mercury limits would reduce coal burning and demand for coal. The bill cushioned this with transition aid for laid-off workers and coal-dependent communities, but the mining industry's interest lay in killing the bill entirely.

Up to 20 percent of emission allowances would be reserved for wind, solar, biomass, efficiency projects and products, and cleaner fossil units, giving these industries a direct revenue stream as cleaner generation becomes cheaper relative to polluting plants.

20 percent of the transition-assistance allowances would be allocated to producers of electricity-intensive goods like metals and chemicals, offsetting higher power prices so the caps would not push their production overseas.
